items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I had the good fortune to interview the trombone player Benny Powell. And he said in his opinion no great art ever came from happiness...

ctx.x: ages. I mean I don’t think he will ever be obsolete. But still I think most people know Louis from the singing he did say during the 1950s to the end of his life than they do from the times when he was breaking through and establishing himself as the future of music. And there was one — Charles — what is his name — one of the great white Civil Rights lawyers had written about how he grew up in Texas in a world of segregation and had assumed all of the things that go with segregation and Jim Crow about…

I had the good fortune to interview the trombone player Benny Powell. And he said in his opinion no great art ever came from happiness — that there had to be adversity for, he said “great art to be formed.” And I wonder how you feel about that?

I don’t think that’s true. That’s one of the myths about art is that you’ve got to be miserable and alienated. That isn’t true at all. I’ve been happy most of my life, not to name myself a great artist but I don’t find that I made better work when I was depressed and miserable than I did when I was happy. I don’t think that’s true of other artists as well. I feel like Cecil Taylor, he wasn’t a miserable person. He was basically in a good mood every time I saw him, most times that I saw him at any rate. Coltrane…
